stem: A client several weeks after total hip arthroplasty reports a sudden painful pop in the operative hip and is now unable to bear weight; the leg appears shortened and abnormally rotated. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.A: Keep the leg in its current position, assess distal neurovascular status, and notify the orthopedic team for urgent evaluation; do not attempt reduction or ambulation.
options.B: Assist the client to stand with a walker and place limited weight on the operative leg to determine whether the prosthetic joint returns to alignment with movement.
options.C: Support the leg while gently rotating and flexing the hip until both legs appear equal in length, then reassess pain and circulation before calling the orthopedic team.
options.D: Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess after the pain improves; if the client can move the foot and toes, defer orthopedic evaluation until the next scheduled visit.

rationale: AAOS identifies prosthetic hip dislocation as a recognized complication of total hip arthroplasty, with the greatest risk during the first few months while tissues are healing, and states that a dislocated prosthetic hip generally requires closed reduction by the treating medical team. AAOS also describes hip dislocation as a medical emergency and advises not moving the injured person. NCBI StatPearls describes posterior hip dislocation as causing a painful pop, inability to ambulate or bear weight, visible shortening/abnormal rotation, and requiring a thorough neurovascular examination. Therefore A is correct. B deliberately mobilizes and loads a suspected dislocated hip, C attempts bedside repositioning instead of medical reduction, and D delays urgent evaluation of an emergency presentation.
educational_objective: Recognize sudden pain, inability to bear weight, and deformity after total hip arthroplasty as possible prosthetic dislocation and prioritize keeping the limb still, focused neurovascular assessment, and urgent orthopedic evaluation without attempting reduction.
source_organization: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), OrthoInfo; National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Total Hip Replacement; Hip Dislocation; Posterior Hip Dislocation — StatPearls
source_version_date: Current AAOS OrthoInfo resources accessed 2026-08-25; StatPearls Posterior Hip Dislocation last updated July 31, 2023 and available in the 2026 StatPearls edition
source_locator: AAOS Total Hip Replacement > Possible Complications of Surgery > Dislocation: the prosthetic ball can come out of the socket; risk is greatest in the first few months while tissues heal; closed reduction usually restores the joint and recurrent cases may require surgery. AAOS Hip Dislocation > Doctor Examination: hip dislocation is a medical emergency, call for help immediately, and do not try to move the injured person; > Treatment > Reduction Procedures: an orthopaedic doctor manipulates the joint back into position under anesthesia or sedation. NCBI StatPearls Posterior Hip Dislocation > History and Physical: painful pop/clunk, inability to ambulate or bear weight, ipsilateral shortening/abnormal rotation, and thorough neurovascular examination before and after reduction.
source_claim_supported: A suspected prosthetic hip dislocation in the early months after arthroplasty requires urgent evaluation, avoidance of unnecessary movement or attempted bedside reduction, and focused neurovascular assessment.

supporting_sources.organization: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), OrthoInfo
supporting_sources.locator: Doctor Examination: hip dislocation is a medical emergency; call for help immediately and do not try to move the injured person. Treatment > Reduction Procedures: reduction is performed by an orthopaedic doctor with anesthesia or sedation.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Suspected hip dislocation warrants urgent medical management and should not be manipulated or mobilized by the nurse.

supporting_sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
supporting_sources.version_date: Last Update: July 31, 2023; available in StatPearls 2026 edition
supporting_sources.locator: History and Physical: a significant clunk or pop followed by pain, inability to ambulate or bear weight, visible ipsilateral shortening with abnormal rotation, and a thorough neurovascular examination at presentation, before and after reduction, and serially thereafter.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: The stem findings are consistent with hip dislocation and neurovascular assessment is a required component of evaluation.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p. 42: reducing the likelihood that clients develop complications related to treatments or procedures; related activity statements include perform focused assessments, recognize trends and changes in client condition and intervene as needed, evaluate client responses to procedures and treatments, and use precautions to prevent injury and/or complications associated with a procedure or diagnosis.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — recognition and urgent escalation of possible prosthetic hip dislocation after total hip arthroplasty
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four actions to eliminate the uniquely-long keyed answer and replace simplistic distractors with realistic near-miss responses involving test ambulation, bedside repositioning, and analgesia with delayed escalation. The final keyed action is limited to source-supported immobilization/no-movement principles, neurovascular assessment, and urgent orthopedic evaluation.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — sudden pop, severe pain, inability to bear weight, shortening and abnormal rotation create a coherent acute-dislocation presentation without requiring unsupported laboratory or imaging assumptions.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly combines urgent escalation, no attempted movement/reduction, and focused neurovascular assessment; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — guarded ambulation may be used in routine rehabilitation, but testing weight bearing in a visibly deformed suspected dislocation conflicts with emergency no-movement guidance.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — supportive handling is appropriate, but actively rotating/flexing the hip to restore alignment constitutes an unapproved reduction attempt.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — analgesia can be appropriate supportive care, but improvement in pain or preserved distal movement does not make a suspected hip dislocation safe for routine follow-up.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only choice that prioritizes protection, neurovascular assessment, and urgent orthopedic evaluation without adding a contraindicated maneuver or delay.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B deliberately loads the joint, C attempts reduction, and D delays emergency evaluation.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four options are essentially identical in length and similar in clinical complexity; the keyed answer is not uniquely detailed.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Reduction of Risk Potential directly includes focused assessment, recognition of condition changes, evaluation after procedures/treatments, and prevention of additional procedure-related injury.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether analgesia first or cautious ambulation could be justified; AAOS characterizes hip dislocation as a medical emergency and advises no movement, while reduction is a clinician-performed procedure and NCBI requires neurovascular assessment, leaving A uniquely best.
